To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the design of functional arrays for light energy capture and charge separation is based on the optimization of the deactivation dynamics of a light-absorbing molecule, by operating on solvent and structure.

1) a careful photophysical characterization of a multicomponent system is essential to identify the preferred deactivation pathway; 2) the solvent can be a key parameter for the optimization of the deactivation step, and 3) the design of the functional multicomponent structure can be achieved by a continuous feedback with the synthesis.

(1) a careful photophysical study, performed by steady-state, time-resolved, and computational spectroscopic techniques, is the starting point of the optimization of functional structures for light energy conversion, (2) the solvent is the first choice to be optimized for the desired deactivation process, and (3) the electronic and nuclear factors of the chromophores and their environment must be continuously optimized by changing the structure/components of the system, via continuous feedback, to achieve the best possible charge separation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new molecular systems for light to chemical conversion and their integration into functional devices.
the development of functional materials for light-to-chemical energy conversion and storage.
the development of new materials for light energy capture and charge separation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the design of functional structures for energy conversion is an iterative process that can be performed by the combined efforts of the synthetic and spectroscopic groups.

, in order to design a functional multicomponent structure for light to chemical conversion, one needs to know the full deactivation pathways of the light-absorption step and the preferred deactivation step to optimize.
the design of functional structures for light to energy conversion is an extremely complex and multidisciplinary process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in a simplified way, the procedure for the design of functional structures for light to charge conversion consists in the following steps: (i) identification of a chromophore with suitable properties, (ii) identification of a preferred deactivation pathway, (iii) optimization of the deactivation pathway, and (iv) construction of a multicomponent structure for light energy capture and charge separation.
, starting from the knowledge of the photophysical properties of the chromophore(s), we can design and synthesize a suitable functional multicomponent system for the desired light energy conversion.

, by combining the knowledge on the photophysical properties of the chromophore and the optimization of the deactivation step (charge separation in this case), it is possible to design and optimize a functional multicomponent structure for light energy conversion, even in the case of a very simple structure, like a donor–acceptor dyad.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rational design of multicomponent systems requires a detailed understanding of the photophysics of the individual components.

, for the optimization of the charge-separation process, the choice of the solvent is not the only factor to be considered, as the electronic and nuclear factors can be modified by operating on the structure of the system, which can be done via continuous feedback between the synthetic chemists and the experimentalists.
a rational and systematic approach can be used for the design of functional multienzyme-like systems, where the individual components are optimized to perform their specific task.
